query: For high-entropy nanoalloys in high-temperature applications, what governs structural and chemical stability, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, propose a controlled comparison that would distinguish it from alternatives, predict observations relative to a baseline, define the boundaries of the prediction, identify supporting evidence from the background, and state a falsifying outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy nanoalloys, the exceptional structural and chemical stability at high temperatures is governed by two interlinked factors: (1) intrinsically sluggish atomic diffusion arising from high configurational entropy that retards grain growth and phase separation, and (2) the thermodynamically driven surface segregation of high-oxygen-affinity constituents (e.g., Al or Cr) which rapidly forms a uniform, self-healing passive oxide layer that protects against further oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic high-entropy nanoalloys (e.g., CoCrFeNiAl or a similar composition) with a single-phase (fcc or bcc) structure and nano-scale grain sizes (typically 20–50 nm) produced by bottom-up synthesis.
generation.intervention: Isothermal thermal aging treatment in a controlled oxidative atmosphere (e.g., air) at high temperatures (e.g., 800–900 °C) for varying durations.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure at 800–900 °C in air, with comparisons made against an inert atmosphere control; nanoalloys maintained in a similar geometric form and grain size distribution to minimize extrinsic effects.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a thin, uniform, self-healing oxide scale (enriched in Al/Cr) on the nanoalloy surface, combined with suppressed grain boundary mobility (verified by minimal grain growth) due to sluggish atomic diffusion.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy retards atomic mobility, which prevents rapid grain coarsening and premature phase separation. Under oxidative environments, the slow diffusion allows selective segregation of high-oxygen-affinity elements to the surface, facilitating quick formation of a protective passive oxide layer that limits further oxygen penetration and chemical degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to conventional nanoalloys or high-entropy bulk alloys with larger grains, the high-entropy nanoalloys will exhibit significantly lower grain growth (e.g., <10% increase in grain size) and form a thinner (e.g., <5 nm), more continuous passive oxide layer after high-temperature exposure. This dual effect mitigates further structural and chemical degradation during prolonged high-temperature operation.
generation.baseline: Nanoalloy samples of similar overall elemental composition but with lower configurational entropy (e.g., binary or ternary nanoalloys) or high-entropy alloys with larger grain sizes, which typically show more pronounced grain coarsening and form thicker, less protective, non-uniform oxide scales under identical conditions.
generation.boundary: This prediction is applicable to high-entropy nanoalloys with equiatomic or near-equiatomic compositions and nano-scale grains (≤50 nm) exposed to temperatures up to ~900 °C. At significantly higher temperatures or for alloys with markedly non-equiatomic distributions, the sluggish diffusion advantage and oxide protective effects may diminish.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative margins (e.g., exact % differences in grain growth or oxide thickness) remain uncertain without direct experiments; the interplay between diffusion kinetics and oxide formation dynamics may be sensitive to minor compositional variations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of nanoalloy samples: one set of high-entropy nanoalloys (equiatomic composition, nano-scale grains) and one set of conventional binary/ternary nanoalloys with similar initial grain sizes. Subject both sets to isothermal aging in air at 900 °C for predetermined durations. Use Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) to measure grain size changes and X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS) along with Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry (SIMS) depth profiling to evaluate the thickness and uniformity of the oxide layer.
measurements: Grain diameter before and after thermal treatment via TEM
Oxide scale thickness and composition via XPS and SIMS
Comparison of oxidation kinetics using thermogravimetric analysis (TGA)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy nanoalloys do not show statistically significantly lower grain growth and a thinner, more uniform passive oxide layer compared to the conventional nanoalloys under identical conditions, then the hypothesis that sluggish diffusion and selective oxide formation govern the enhanced high-temperature stability is rejected.
